(p-45) (Surah 21: al-Anbiya' (The Prophets) is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and twelve.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 3:

﴿Their hearts are heedless.﴾ That is, they listened to it while combining mockery, frivolity and inattention to reflecting upon it. It is also permissible that it be from the waw of ﴿they play﴾. It has been read in the nominative (ليهية, lāhiyatun), on the basis that it is another predicate of the pronoun. ﴿And they conspired in secret, the conversation.﴾ They went to great lengths in concealing it, or they made it such that their private discussion of it was hidden. ﴿Those who did wrong﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the waw of ﴿and they conspired﴾, to indicate that they are wrongdoers in what they concealed. Or it is its subject (fa'il), with the waw serving as the sign of the plural. Or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the preceding clause, and its original form was "and these people conspired in secret," so the relative pronoun was placed in its position, to record upon their action that it is wrongdoing. Or it is in the accusative on the basis of censure (dhamm). ﴿"Is this anything but a human being like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?"﴾ With his command, it is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for ﴿the conversation﴾, or as an object (maf'ul) of an implied saying, as if they reasoned from his being a human being to his lying in claiming prophethood, because they believed that the Messenger could only be an angel. And they inferred from this that what he brought of extraordinary events, such as the Qur'an, is magic, so they denied its presence. They conspired in secret only in order to deliberate on devising what would demolish his affair and expose its corruption to people in general.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 4–5:

﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heavens and the earth"﴾, whether spoken aloud or in secret, let alone what they conceal, so this is more emphatic than His words ﴿Say: "He who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth has sent it down"﴾. For this reason it was chosen here, and to match His words ﴿and they conspired in secret, the wrongdoers﴾ in intensity. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read ﴿qala﴾ (He said) in the form of reporting about the Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, so nothing that they whisper or harbour is hidden from Him.

﴿Rather they say: "A confusion of dreams! Rather he has invented it! Rather he is a poet!"﴾ This is a shifting (idrab) from their saying that it is magic to saying that it is a jumble of dreams, then to saying that it is speech he has fabricated, then to saying that it is the speech of a poet. The apparent meaning is that the first ﴿bal﴾ marks the completion of one report and the beginning of another, or it marks a shift away from their disputing about the Messenger (ﷺ) and the signs that appeared through him to their idle talk about the matter of the Qur'an. The second and third ﴿bal﴾ mark their shift from its being false fancies that were imagined to him and mixed up in him, to its being fabrications that he invented of his own accord, and then to its being poetic speech that conjures up in the listener meanings that have no reality and makes him desire them. It is also possible that all of these are from God, as a depiction of their statements descending through degrees of corruption, because its being poetry is further removed than its being fabrication, since it is laden with truths and wisdom and contains nothing resembling the speech of poets. Its being dreams is further removed than both, since it includes many unseen matters that corresponded to reality, whereas a fabricator would not be like this, unlike dreams. Also, they had tested the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for over forty years and never heard a lie from him at all. Its being magic is further removed still, since it is of the same kind as magic in that both are extraordinary events.

﴿So let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent﴾, that is, as the earlier ones were sent with it, such as the white hand, the staff, healing the blind and the leper, and raising the dead. The correctness of the comparison lies in the fact that being sent implies bringing a sign.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 6–7:

﴿Not one town before them, which We destroyed, believed.﴾ "Town" here means the people of a town. ﴿We destroyed﴾ them for demanding signs when they came to them. ﴿Will they then believe?﴾ Even if you brought them such signs, while they are more obstinate than those (before them). In this there is a warning that withholding the demanded sign was for the sake of sparing them. For if it were brought and they did not believe, they would deserve the punishment of annihilation, as those before them did.

﴿We sent not before you any but men to whom We revealed (Our message). So ask the People of the Reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ This is a reply to their saying ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ So He commanded them to ask the People of the Book (ahl al-Kitab) about the condition of the earlier messengers, so that doubt and suspicion would be removed from them. The referral to them is either as a form of argument against them, since the polytheists used to consult them about the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ) and trusted their word, or because the report of a large multitude (khabar al-jamm al-ghafir, a mass-transmitted report) necessarily produces knowledge, even if they were disbelievers.

Hafs read ﴿nūḥī﴾ with the nun (i.e., "We reveal," in the first person plural).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 8–10:

﴿We did not make them a body that does not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾ This negates what they believed, that these are among the distinctive features of the angel, from the messengers, as an affirmation (tahqiq) that they were mortal humans like them. It was also said that it is a response to their saying, ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ ﴿Nor were they immortal﴾ is an emphasis and confirmation of it, for sustaining life by food is among the consequences of dissolution (tahlil, decomposition), which leads to annihilation. The singular "body" (jasad) is not intended as a genus. It is either because it is originally a verbal noun, or by omitting a modifier, or by interpreting the pronoun as referring to each one. The body is a colored substance, which is why it is not applied to water and air, and from it comes "jasad" for saffron. It was also said that it is a composite body, because its root means gathering a thing and strengthening it.

﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them﴾ meaning, regarding the promise. ﴿So We saved them and whom We willed﴾ meaning the believers among them, and whoever in whose preservation there is wisdom, like one who will believe, he or one of his descendants. For this reason the Arabs were protected from the punishment of extirpation (isti'sal). ﴿And We destroyed the extravagant﴾ in disbelief and sins.

﴿Indeed We have sent down to you﴾ O Quraysh, ﴿a Book﴾ meaning the Qur'an. ﴿In it is your remembrance﴾ your renown, like His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾; or your admonition; or what you seek through it of good repute from noble character. ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ so that you believe.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 11–13:

﴿And how many a town have We shattered, which was wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ [Shattered (qasama) is used because qasm means a break that shows the parts no longer fit together, unlike fasm (a clean cut).]

﴿Which was wrongdoing﴾ is an attribute of its people; it is attributed to the town because the town has been put in the place of its people. ﴿And We brought into being after it﴾ after the destruction of its people. ﴿Another people﴾ in their place.

﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾ when they realized the severity of Our punishment with the perception of one who witnesses it directly. The pronoun refers to the people, which is omitted here but implied.

﴿Behold, they were fleeing from it﴾ running away swiftly, spurring their mounts, or likened to those who spur their mounts because of the extremity of their haste.

﴿Do not flee﴾ this is by way of an implied saying: it was said to them mockingly, "Do not flee," either through the tongue of circumstance or through speech. The speaker is an angel or one of the believers present there. ﴿And return to what you were made to enjoy in luxury therein﴾ the luxury, pleasure and delight; itrāf means squandering the blessing.

﴿And to your dwellings﴾ which were yours. ﴿Perhaps you will be questioned﴾ tomorrow about your deeds, or you will be punished, since questioning is one of the preliminaries of punishment; or you will be summoned for questioning and consultation about urgent matters and calamities.

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, on Surah 21, verses 14–15:

﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ When they saw the punishment and saw no way of escape, this (their repentance) did not benefit them. It is also said that the people of Hadur, a town in the villages of Yemen, were sent a prophet, but they killed him. So God gave power over them to Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), who put the sword among them. A caller from the sky cried out, "O avengers of the prophets!" Then they regretted and said that.

﴿And that remained their cry﴾. They kept repeating it. He called it a "cry" (*da'wa*) because the one who wails seems to be calling out to Woe (*al-wayl*), saying, "O Woe, come, for this is your time." Each of ﴿تِلْكَ﴾ (*tilka*, "that") and ﴿دَعْواهُم﴾ (*da'wahum*, "their cry") may be read as a noun (*ismiyya*) or as a predicate (*khabariyya*). ﴿Until We made them like a harvest﴾, like mown crops, and *haseed* means mown plant. For this reason it (*haseed*) is not made plural. ﴿Extinguished﴾, dead, from *khamadat al-nar* ("the fire went out"). Together with ﴿haseedan﴾, it occupies the position of the second object (*al-maf'ul al-thani*), as in your saying, "We made him sweet and sour," since the meaning is: "We made them gathered together, because of the likeness between being mown and being extinguished." Or it is an adjective of it, or a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of its pronoun.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 16–17:

﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ Rather, We created them filled with varieties of wonders, as a means of insight for the observers (al-nuzzar), a reminder for those of discernment, and a cause through which the affairs of the servants are ordered, in their livelihood (ma'ash) and in their return (ma'ad, the afterlife). So they should ascend through them to the attainment of perfection, and not be deceived by their adornments, for they are swiftly passing away.

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾: that by which one amuses oneself and plays. ﴿We would have taken it from Our presence﴾: from Our power, or from Us, of what befits Our presence, of immaterial beings (mujarradat), not of raised bodies and extended masses, as is your custom in raising ceilings, decorating them, and arranging and adorning carpets. It is said that al-lahw means "child" in the dialect of Yemen, and it is said "wife." The intended meaning is a refutation of the Christians. ﴿If We were doing (that)﴾ (p-48): and this indicates the answer to the answer mentioned earlier. It is said that "in" (in) is negative, and the sentence is like the conclusion of the conditional clause.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 18:

﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes.﴾ This is a turning away from taking up idle play (lahw), and an affirmation that Allah is exalted above play (la'ib). That is: rather, it is within Our way to overcome the truth, of which seriousness (jidd) is a part, over falsehood, of which idle play is among the number. ﴿Then it crushes it﴾, that is, it annihilates it. He has used for this the metaphor of "hurling" (qadhf), which is a distant throwing and entails the solidity of the target, and "crushing" (damgh), which is breaking the brain such that its membrane is split, leading to the departure of the soul, to depict its nullification by it and to emphasize it. It has also been read as «fayadmaghahu» in the accusative, as in the verse of the poet:

"I will leave my dwelling to the Banu Tamim... and I will go to the Hijaz and rest."

Its justification, despite its weakness, is taking it according to the meaning and coordinating it with "the truth" (al-haqq). ﴿And behold, it is vanishing﴾, that is, destroyed; and zuhuq is the departure of the soul. He mentioned it to reinforce the metaphor (tarshih al-majaz). ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾, for what you attribute to Him, of what is not permissible for Him. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and "ma" is either verbal-masdar (mașdariyyah), relative (mawsulah), or descriptive (mawsufah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 19–20:

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ by way of creation and ownership. ﴿And those who are with Him﴾ means the angels brought near to Him, who, because of their honour before Him, hold the station of those who are drawn near to kings. It is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with ﴿whoever is in the heavens﴾. Its singular form, إفرادُهُ (*ifraduhu*, "its being singular"), is either for glorification, or because it is more general than the preceding phrase in one respect, or the intended meaning is a category of angels exalted above settling in the heavens and the earth. Alternatively, it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is: ﴿They do not disdain to worship Him﴾, meaning they do not consider themselves too great for it. ﴿Nor do they tire﴾, meaning they do not grow weary of it. The word يَسْتَحْسِرُونَ (*yastahsiruna*, "they grow weary") was used rather than الحُسُور (*husur*, "weariness"), though *istihsar* is the stronger form, to draw attention to the fact that their worship, given its weight and its continuity, truly merits that one should become weary of it, yet they do not become weary.

﴿They glorify Him night and day﴾, meaning they declare Him far above imperfection and exalt Him constantly. ﴿They never slacken﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, "state qualifier") from the waw of يُسَبِّحُونَ (*yusabbihuna*, "they glorify"). It may also be a resumptive new sentence (*istinaf*), or a circumstantial clause from a pronoun before it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 21–23:

﴿Or have they taken gods﴾ "Bal" (rather), "they have taken," and the hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying their taking them. ﴿from the earth﴾ is an adjective modifying "gods," or it is connected to the verb in the sense of origination (*ibtida'*, origin or starting point). Its benefit is belittlement (*tahqir*), not restriction (*takhsis*). ﴿They raise the dead﴾: although they did not state this explicitly, it follows that they ascribed divinity to these gods, since among the necessary attributes of divinity is power over all possibilities. The purpose is to show their ignorance and to mock them. For emphasis on this, the pronoun "they" (*hum*) was added, which gives the impression that raising the dead is restricted to them.

﴿If there were in them gods other than God﴾: "other than" is described with "illa" (except), because an exception (*istithna'*) is not possible here, since what precedes it does not include what follows it. Its indication is that corruption is necessarily entailed by the existence of gods in them besides Him. The intended meaning is that corruption is necessarily entailed by their being gods in an absolute sense, or together with Him, treating "other" (*ghayr*) as in the exception with *ghayr*, treating it as a governing term. The nominative reading as a substitute (*badal*) is not permitted, because it is a branch of the exception and is conditional on the sentence being negative, not affirmative (*muwjab*). ﴿would have been corrupted﴾: would have been ruined, because of the disagreement and mutual opposition that would exist between them. If they agreed on the purpose, the decrees would be pursued by it; if they disagreed about it, they would obstruct one another from it. ﴿Glory be to God, Lord of the Throne﴾: the one who encompasses all bodies, who is the locus of arrangements and the origin of decrees. ﴿above what they describe﴾: from ascribing partners, consorts, and offspring to Him.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾: because of His greatness, the strength of His authority, His singularity in divinity, and His self-originated sovereignty. ﴿but they will be questioned﴾: because they are (p-49)

servants who are owned and enslaved. The pronoun (*al-damir*) refers either to "gods" (*alihah*) or to "the servants" (*al-'ibad*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 24:

﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him?﴾ He repeated it to magnify their disbelief, to express horror at their affair, to rebuke them, and to show their ignorance. Or (the repetition) combines the denial of what would be a support for them from transmitted testimony with the denial of what would be a proof for them from reason, in the sense: "They produced gods who raise the dead, so they took them as gods, because of what they found in them of the special attributes of divinity." Or: "They found in the divine Books the command to associate others with Him, so they took them (as gods) in compliance with the command." This is reinforced by the fact that He arranged, for the first, what indicates its corruption by reason, and for the second, what indicates its corruption by transmission.

﴿Say: Bring your proof.﴾ For this, either from reason or from transmission, since a claim without evidence is not valid. How could it be, when the arguments have agreed on its falsehood, both by reason and by transmission?

﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me.﴾ That is, from the heavenly Books. Look, do you find in them anything but the command to monotheism (tawhid) and the prohibition of associating partners? Since monotheism does not depend for its soundness on the sending of messengers and the sending down of Books, it is valid to argue for it by transmission. "Those with me" means his community, and "those before me" means the earlier nations. The addition of "reminder" (dhikr) to them is because it is their admonition. It has also been read with tanwin and with the governing function (i'mal), and with it and with "min" (from) as a genitive particle, on the basis that "ma'a" (with) in the phrase is an adverbial noun like "qabl" (before) and "ba'd" (after) and the like, and also without them.

﴿Rather, most of them do not know the truth.﴾ And they do not distinguish between it and falsehood. It has also been read as "al-haqqu" in the nominative, on the basis that it is a deleted predicate, a intermediate (wasat) for emphasis between the cause and the effect.

﴿So they are turning away.﴾ From monotheism and following the Messenger, because of that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 25–27:

﴿And We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾ This is a generalization after a specification, since the phrase "those before me" (ذِكْرُ مَن قَبْلِي), insofar as it is a predicate of the demonstrative noun, is specific to those present among them, namely the three Books. Ḥafṣ, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿nūḥī ilayhi﴾ with the nūn and a kasra on the ḥā', while the rest read it with the yā' and a fatḥa on the ḥā'.

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken a son.﴾ It was revealed concerning Khuzā'ah, who said: the angels are the daughters of Allah. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾: a declaration of His transcendence above that. ﴿Rather, they are servants﴾: rather, they are servants insofar as they are created, and they are not offspring. ﴿Honoured﴾: brought near (muqarrabūn), and in this is an indication of the refutation of those people. It is also read with the shaddah.

﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾: they do not say anything until He has said it, as is the custom of well-mannered servants. Its original form is: "their speech does not precede His speech," so the precedence is attributed to Him and to them, and speech is made its locus and instrument, as an alerting to the reprehensibility of precedence, which is aimed at those who speak against Allah what He has not said. The lām has been substituted for the idafa, for brevity and to avoid repeating the pronoun. It is also read "lā yusbaqūnahu" with a ḍammah, from sābaqtuhu, fa-sabaqtuhu, asbiquhu. ﴿And they act by His command﴾: they never do anything He has not commanded them to do.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 30:

﴿Have not those who disbelieve seen﴾ — or: "have they not known?" Ibn Kathir read it without the waw (ا.e. "a-lam yarā" without the conjunction waw). ﴿that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass﴾ — meaning possessors of a joined state, or joined (martuqatayn), and ratq is joining and cohesion; that is, they were one thing and one united reality. ﴿Then We separated them﴾ — by diversifying and distinguishing them. Or, the heavens were one and were then split (futiqat) by the various movements until they became spheres (aflak), and the earths were one and were made, by the difference of their qualities and conditions, into layers (tabaqat) or climes (aqalim). It has also been said: they were such that there was no gap between them, so a gap was made. It has also been said: they were a joined mass that did not rain nor produce plants, so We split them by rain and plants; in this case the word "the heavens" refers to the lowest heaven, and its plural form is in view of the horizons; or "the heavens" refers to their secrets, on the basis that they have some part in rain. The disbelievers, even if they do not know this, are able to know it by reflection, for splitting is an accident requiring an influencing agent, which is necessary either directly or through an intermediary; or by inquiry of the scholars and by consulting books. He said "were" and did not say "be," because what is meant is the collectivity of the heavens and the collectivity of the earth. It has been read "ratqan" with a fatha, on the presumption of "shay'an ratqan," i.e. a thing that was joined, like "al-rafḍ" in the sense of "al-marfūḍ" (the rejected). ﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ — and We created from water every animal, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah created every creature from water﴾; this is because it is among its greatest constituents, or because of the extreme need for it and benefit from it in its very essence; or We made every living thing by means of a cause from water without which it would not live. It has been read "ḥayyan" (living) as an attribute of "kull" or as a second object, and the adverbial phrase is superfluous, and "shay'" (thing) is restricted to animals. (﴿Will they not then believe?﴾) despite the manifestness of the signs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 31–32:

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains﴾, steadfast (ثابِتاتٍ, *thābitāt*), from *rasā al-shay'* (رَسا الشَّيْءُ), meaning a thing became fixed when it settled. ﴿Lest it should sway with them﴾: out of aversion to its leaning with them and being agitated. It has also been said that the meaning is ﴿lest it should not sway with them﴾, so that *lā* (لا, "not") was omitted, because there is no risk of confusion. ﴿And We placed in it﴾, that is, in the earth or in the mountains, ﴿broad paths﴾, wide routes (مَسالِكَ واسِعَةً). He placed *fijājan* (فِجاجًا), which is a description of *subulan* (سُبُلًا), before it in order that it become a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*, حالًا, a grammatical term for an adverbial accusative describing the state of a noun), which indicates that when He created them, He created them in this state. Or [He placed it first] so that *subulan* would be a substitute (*badal*, بَدَلٌ, a grammatical term for an appositive substitute) for *minhā* (مِنها), which implicitly indicates that He created them and widened them for travelers, together with the emphasis that this carries. ﴿So that they may be guided﴾ to their interests.

﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾, protected from falling by His power, or from decay and dissolution until the appointed time by His will, or from eavesdropping by means of shooting stars. ﴿Yet they turn away from its signs﴾, from its conditions, which indicate the existence of the Creator, His oneness, the perfection of His power, and the boundlessness of His wisdom. Some of these are perceived by the senses, and others are investigated in the two sciences of natural philosophy (*ʿilm al-ṭabīʿah*, عِلْمِ الطَّبِيعَةِ) and astronomy (*al-hay'ah*, الهَيْئَةِ). ﴿Turning away﴾, not reflecting.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 33:

﴿And He it is Who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ is an explanation of some of those signs. ﴿Each in an orbit﴾ — i.e., each one of them. The tanwin here is a substitute for the genitive noun that was omitted (the idafa's second term), and what is meant by "orbit" (falak) is the genus, as in their saying: "The amir clothed them with a robe (ḥulla)." ﴿Swimming﴾ — they hasten over the surface of the orbit as a swimmer hastens over the surface of water. This is the predicate of "each" (kull), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the sun and the moon." Their being singled out with this predicate is permissible because there is no ambiguity, and the pronoun refers to both of them. The plural was used in view of the risings (maṭāli'), and the pronoun was made the waw of rational beings because swimming is an action of rational beings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 34–35:

﴿We did not grant immortality to any human before you. So if you die, will they be the ones who remain forever?﴾ It was revealed when they said, "We await for him the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)." And in its meaning is his (the poet's) saying:

"Say to those who gloat over us: Wake up! The gloaters will meet what we have met."

The fa' (in fa-in) is for linking the conditional to what precedes it, and the hamza (in a-fa-in) is for denouncing their claim after this has been established.

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾: tasting the bitterness of its separation from its body; and this is a proof of what they denied. ﴿And We test you﴾: We deal with you as one who is being tested. ﴿With evil and with good﴾: with calamities and blessings. ﴿As a trial﴾: ibtila' (testing), a verbal noun (masdar) from a verb other than its own root. ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾: so We will recompense you according to the patience and gratitude found in you. In this there is an allusion that the purpose of this life, of testing, and of exposing people to reward and punishment is to establish what has preceded.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 36–37:

﴿And when those who disbelieve see you, they do not take you except for mockery.﴾ "Except as one mocked" (muhza'an bihi). And they say: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ That is, with evil. He stated it without qualification because of the indication of the context (dalalat al-hal), for mentioning an enemy is only done with evil. ﴿And they, at the mention of the Most Merciful﴾ with the Oneness of God (tawhid), or by guiding creation through the sending of messengers and the sending down of books as a mercy upon them, or by the Qur'an. ﴿They are disbelievers﴾ deniers. Therefore they are more deserving of being mocked. The repetition of the pronoun is for emphasis, for specification, and to separate the relative clause from the predicate.

﴿Man was created of haste.﴾ It is as if he was created from it, because of his excessive hastiness and his lack of steadiness, like your saying: "Zayd was created from generosity." What is inherent in him is made as if it were what he was molded upon, and it is from him, as an exaggeration of its being necessary for him. For this reason it has been said that this is an inversion (qalb) of the expression. And from his haste is his rushing to disbelief and his seeking the threat hastily.

It has been narrated that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he sought the punishment hastily.

﴿I will show you My signs﴾ My retributions in this world, like the event of Badr, and in the Hereafter the punishment of the Fire. ﴿So do not ask Me to hasten them.﴾ By bringing them. The prohibition is against what their souls have been disposed toward, so that it may restrain them from their aim.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 38–40:**

﴿And they say, "When is this promise?"﴾ That is, the time of the promise of punishment or of the Resurrection. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ They mean the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿If only those who disbelieve knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces or from their backs, nor will they be helped﴾. The answer (jawab) of "law" (if only) is omitted, and "ḥīna" (the time when) is the direct object (maf'ul) of "ya'lamu" (knows). That is: if only they knew the time they are seeking to hasten by their saying, ﴿When is this promise?﴾, which is the time when the Fire will surround them from every side, such that they will not be able to repel it, nor will they find a helper to prevent it, for what they hastened. It is also permissible that the object of "ya'lamu" be left unstated, and that a verb be implied for "ḥīna" with the meaning: if they had knowledge, they would not have hastened, knowing (p-52) the falsity of what they are upon at the time when they cannot ward it off. The apparent noun has been placed here in the position of the pronoun to indicate what caused them to be in that condition.

﴿Rather, it will come upon them﴾ the promise, or the Fire, or the Hour. ﴿Suddenly﴾ unexpectedly; it is either a verbal noun (maṣdar) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It has also been recited as "baghtatan" with a fatḥah on the ghayn. ﴿And it will confound them﴾ it will overpower them or bewilder them. Both verbs have been recited with the yā' (as "yaʾtīhim" and "yabhatuhum"), and the pronoun refers to "al-wa'd" (the promise) or "al-ḥīn" (the time). The same applies to His saying ﴿so they will not be able to avert it﴾, because "al-wa'd" means the Fire or the promise, and "al-ḥīn" means the Hour. It is also permissible that the pronoun refer to "al-nār" (the Fire) or to "baghtatan" (suddenly).

﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾ they will not be given respite. In this there is a reminder of the respite given to them in this world.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 41–42:

﴿And certainly were messengers before you mocked, so there befell those who mocked among them what they used to mock at.﴾ It is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is a promise to him that what they do to him will rebound upon them, just as what befell those who mocked the prophets, namely their recompense, befell those who did what they did.

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to those who mock: ﴿Who protects you﴾, guards you, ﴿by night and day from the Most Merciful﴾, from His punishment should He intend it for you? **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 43–44:**

﴿Or do they have gods who protect them from Us?﴾ Rather, do they have gods who protect them from a punishment that surpasses Our protection, or from a punishment that comes from Us? The two shifts (*idrab*, a turning from one matter to another) away from the question concern the order of the matter, for it is far from one who is turned away and heedless of a thing, and even farther from one who holds the opposite belief. ﴿They cannot help themselves, nor will they be accompanied by Us.﴾ This is a resumption (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins afresh) that nullifies what they believed, for one who cannot help himself, and is not accompanied by help from Allah, how could he help another?

﴿Rather, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until a long life passed over them.﴾ This is a shift (*idrab*) from what they imagined, by stating what is the cause of their being preserved, namely *istidraj* (gradual leading on, respite) and enjoyment through the lifespans decreed for them. Or it is a shift from indicating its falsehood, by stating what caused them to imagine that. That is, Allah gave them enjoyment in the worldly life and granted them respite until their lifespans grew long, so they reckoned that they would always remain thus, and that this was due to what they were upon. For this reason He follows it with what shows that it is a false hope, and He says: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land﴾, the land of the disbelievers, ﴿reducing it from its extremities?﴾ by giving the Muslims power over it. This is a depiction of what Allah brings about at the hands of the Muslims. ﴿Are they then the victors?﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers are the victors.

﴿Say, "I only warn you by the revelation."﴾ By that which has been revealed to me. ﴿But the deaf do not hear the call﴾ Ibn ʿAmir recited it as (وَلا تُسْمِعُ الصُّمَّ) (wa-la tusmiʿu al-summa, "and you do not make the deaf hear"), addressing the Prophet ﷺ, and it was also read with the yaʾ (يَسْمَعُ, "they do not hear"), on the basis that it contains his pronoun. He called them "the deaf" and placed this in the position of their pronoun in order to indicate their deafness and their failure to benefit from what they hear. ﴿when they are warned﴾ is in the accusative governed by (يَسْمَعُ, "hear") or by (الدُّعاءَ, "the call"). Its restriction to this is because the discourse concerns warning, or for emphasis on their deafness and their audacity.

﴿And if a breath of the punishment of your Lord touches them﴾ anything at all. Within it there are intensifications: he mentioned "touch" (مَسّ), and the word "breath" (نَفْحَة) carries the sense of paucity, since the original meaning of (النَّفْح) is the wafting of the scent of a thing, and the pattern (البِناء) indicates a single instance. ﴿of your Lord's punishment﴾ of that with which they are being warned. ﴿they will surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ They would call down woe upon themselves and confess their wrongdoing against themselves.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 47:

﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice (al-qist), (meaning) the justice by which the books of deeds are weighed.﴾ It was also said that the setting up of the scales is a metaphor for the establishment of a righteous reckoning, and that recompense is according to deeds, with justice. The singular "al-qist" is used because it is a verbal noun (masdar) described by the word, for emphasis (li'l-mubalaghah).

﴿For the Day of Resurrection⦆ — for the recompense of the Day of Resurrection, or for its people, or "in it," like your saying: "I came on the fifth of the month" (ji'tu li-khamsin khalawna min al-shahr).

﴿So no soul will be wronged in anything⦆ — of its right, or of wrongdoing (min al-zulm).

﴿And if there is the weight of a grain of mustard seed⦆ — i.e., even if the deed or the wrong is the amount of a grain. Nafi' read "mithqal" in the nominative as the complete (tammah) form of "kana" ("there is").

﴿We will bring it forth⦆ — We will present it. It was read "atayna" (we gave), meaning "We will repay with it," from the giving (al-iytaʾ), for it is close to "a'taynā" (we gave); or from al-mu'atah (reciprocation), for they brought Him their deeds and He brought them recompense. "Athabna" (We reward) and "jiʾna" (We bring) are also related. The pronoun refers to "mithqal," and its feminine form is due to its being construed with "habbah" (grain).

﴿And sufficient is We as reckoners⦆ — for there is no addition to Our knowledge and Our justice.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 48–50:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion (al-Furqan), and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing﴾. That is, the Book that combines being a criterion (furqan) distinguishing truth from falsehood; and "a light" (diya') by which one is guided out of the darkness of bewilderment and ignorance; and "a reminder" (dhikr) by which the God-fearing take admonition, or [it is a reminder in that] it mentions what they need of the laws (shara'i'). It has been said that "the Criterion" (al-Furqan) means victory, and it has been said it means the splitting of the sea. It is also read as "diya'" without a waw, on the basis that it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) relative to "al-Furqan."

﴿Those who fear their Lord unseen﴾: this is an attributive description of "the God-fearing," or a praise of them, in the accusative or nominative case. ("Unseen," bil-ghayb) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring either to the subject (the agent) or to the object. ﴿And they are apprehensive of the Hour﴾: "apprehensive" (mushfiqun) means fearful. Placing the pronoun first and building the predicate upon it carries emphasis and an allusion.

﴿And this is a reminder﴾: meaning the Qur'an. ﴿Blessed﴾: abundant in its good. ﴿That We have sent down﴾: upon Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿Will you then deny it?﴾: an interrogative of rebuke.

﴿And We had already given Ibrahim his rushd (right guidance)﴾: the guidance to the aspects of righteousness. Its attribution to him (in the form "his rushd") serves to indicate that it is a rushd like no other, and that he had a standing (sha'n) of his own.

It is also recited as (rushdahu) with a different vowelling, and this is a dialect form (lughah). ﴿From before﴾: from before (the time of) Musa and Harun, or before Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: from before his prophethood (istinba'), or before his reaching maturity (bulugh), when he said: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face﴾ and ﴿We had knowledge of him﴾: We knew that he was worthy of what We had given him, or that he was one who combined the excellent qualities and noble characteristics. In this is an indication that the act of Allah, glorified and exalted is by choice and wisdom, and that He has knowledge of particulars.

﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾: this is connected to (ataynā, "We gave") or to (rushdahu, "his rushd") or to an implied element, i.e. "Mention of the times of his rushd, the time when he said:" ﴿What are these images to which you are devoted?﴾ This is a belittling of their status and a rebuke for their reverence of them, for an image (timthal) is a form with no spirit in it, which neither harms nor benefits. The lam here indicates particularity (ikhtisas), not transitivity (ta'diyah), since the transitive verb for "devotion" (ukuf) takes (ʿalā). The meaning is: you are the ones performing devotion to them. It is permissible to interpret it with (ʿalā), or to make ukuf imply the meaning of worship (ʿibadah).(p-54)

﴿They said: We found our fathers worshipping them﴾: so we imitated them. This is an answer to what the question implied, namely the inquiry about what required their worship and what compelled them to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 54–56:

﴿He said: "You and your fathers have certainly been in clear error."﴾ They were enrolled in a thread of error that is not hidden from any person of intellect, because neither party relied on any proof. Taqlid (blind imitation), if it is permissible at all, is permissible only for one who knows in general that the one he follows is upon the truth.

﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ As if, by their considering it unlikely that he was misguiding them, they supposed that what he said he said in a spirit of play, so they said: "Do you say it in earnest, or are you joking with it?"

﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them."﴾ This is a turning away from his being a jester, by establishing the proof for what he claimed. The pronoun "hunna" refers either to the heavens and the earth, or to the images. And this is more effective in misguiding them and in establishing the argument against them. ﴿And I am of those who bear witness to that﴾, i.e., to the aforementioned tawhid (oneness of God). ﴿Among the witnesses﴾, i.e., among those who have verified it and who furnish proof for it, for the witness (shahid) is one who has verified a thing and established it.

﴿By Allah!﴾ It is also read with the particle بِ (bi-), which is the original form. The تَ (ta') is a substitute for the واو (waw), which was itself substituted from the بِ, and it carries the sense of wonder (taʿajjub). ﴿Surely I will scheme against your idols﴾: I will exert myself to break them. The word الكَيْد (kayd, scheming) and the wonder conveyed by the تَ are used because the matter is difficult and depends on a kind of stratagem. ﴿After you have turned away﴾ from them. ﴿Going off﴾ to your festival. ﴿So he reduced them to fragments﴾: قُطاعًا (qutaʿan, pieces). The word جُذاذًا (judhadhan) is on the pattern فُعالٌ (fuʿal) in the sense of مَفْعُولٌ (maf'ul, "that which is broken"), like الحُطام (hutam, debris), from the root الجَذّ (jadhdh), which means cutting. Al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra (judhadhin), which is a dialectal form, or it is the plural of جَذِيذٌ (jadhidh), like خِفافٌ (khifaf) from خَفِيفٌ (khafif). It was also read with a fatha: "judhadhan," the plural of جَذِيذٌ, and "jadhadhan," the plural of جَذَّةٌ (jadhdhah). ﴿Except a big one among them﴾: for the idols, he broke the rest and spared it, and he put the axe on its neck. ﴿That they might return to it﴾: because he was confident that they would return only to him, since he was singled out and well known for his enmity toward their gods. Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 21, verses 62–63:

﴿They said: "Did you do this to our gods, O Ibrahim?"﴾ when they had brought him (before them).

﴿He said: "Rather, this one, their chief, did it. So ask them, if they can speak."﴾ He ascribed the act to him (the chief) in a figurative manner (*tajawwuz*, metaphorical attribution), because his anger at their increased veneration of him caused him to be the reason for the act, since he was the one who directly carried it out. Or (he ascribed it to him) as an affirmation of himself, together with mockery and rebuke, in an allusive style (*ta'ridi*, indirect implication), as when someone who cannot write well says to you, regarding something you wrote in a fine hand: "Did you write this?" and you reply: "Rather, you wrote it yourself." Or (it is) a report of what their position (*madhhab*, doctrinal stance) necessarily entails as permissible. It has been said that the phrase in meaning is connected to His words ﴿if they can speak﴾, and that what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraḍ*). Or it refers back to the pronoun in (*fata*, "youth") or (Ibrahim). His words ﴿their chief, this one﴾ are a subject and predicate (*mubtada' wa khabar*), and for this reason one pauses at his (the chief's) act.

As for what is related, that he (upon him be blessings and peace) said: "Ibrahim told three lies," (this is) a naming of allusive speech as lying, because its outward form resembles his (Ibrahim's) form.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 66–68:

﴿He said: "Do you then worship, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ This is a denunciation of their worship of them after they had acknowledged that they are inanimate objects that neither benefit nor harm, for that contradicts divinity (al-uluhiyyah).

﴿Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides Allah!﴾ It is an expression of his exasperation at their persistence in manifest falsehood. ﴿Uff﴾ is the sound made by one who is exasperated, and its meaning is ugliness and foulness. ﴿They said﴾ — resorting to harm, since they were unable to argue. ﴿"Burn him"﴾ — for fire is the most terrifying punishment with which one can be punished. ﴿"And support your gods"﴾ — by avenging them. ﴿"If you are going to act"﴾ — if you are going to be supporters of them with firm support. The one speaking among them was a man from the Kurds of Persia named Hayun, who was swallowed up by the earth; and it is said that he was Nimrod.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 69:

﴿We said: O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾. [It is] "coolness and safety," i.e., "Be cool, [without causing] harm." In this there are intensifications: the fire, which is subjugated to His power, is made obedient and submissive, and "Be" (kūnī) with [the predicate] "coolness" is put in the place of "be cool" (ubrudī). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 78–79:

﴿And [remember] Dawud and Sulayman, when they gave judgment concerning the tilth﴾ (al-harth), that is, the crops; and it was said: concerning a vineyard whose clusters hung low. ﴿When the people's flock had strayed into it at night and grazed it﴾ (nafashat), that is, it grazed it by night. ﴿And We were witness to their judgment﴾ (li-hukmihim), to the judgment of the judges and of those who came before them for judgment, [We were] knowing.

﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾: the pronoun refers either to the judgment (al-hukumah) or to the ruling (al-fatwa). It is also read as «fa-afhamnaha».

It is related that Dawud ruled that the flock should go to the owner of the tilth. Sulayman, who was eleven years old at the time, said: "Other than this is more gentle on both of them." So he ordered that the flock be handed over to the people of the tilth, to benefit from its milk, its young and its wool, and that the tilth be handed over to the owners of the flock, who would tend it until it returned to its former state, after which the two would exchange (back).

Perhaps the two of them spoke by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning). The first ruling is analogous to the view of Abu Hanifa concerning the slave who commits an offence, and the second is like the view of al-Shafi'i on requiring compensation for the deprivation (al-haylulah) in the case of a usurped slave who has run away. Its ruling in our law, according to al-Shafi'i, is that the owner must compensate for what is destroyed at night, since it is customary to keep animals under control at night. Likewise the Prophet ﷺ ruled when the she-camel of al-Bara' entered an orchard and damaged it: «The owners of property must guard it by day, and the owners of livestock must guard it by night.»

According to Abu Hanifa, there is no liability unless a guard is with it, based on his ﷺ saying: «The wound inflicted by an animal is unrequited (jubar).»

﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾: this is evidence that the error of a mujtahid does not discredit him. It was also said that it is evidence that every mujtahid is correct; but this contradicts the implication of His words: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾. Were it not for the transmitted report, it would be possible that their two judgments agreed, and that His words ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Sulayman﴾ are to show what He favoured him with in his youth.

﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Us] along with Dawud, and the birds﴾ (yusabbihna), that is, they proclaim God's holiness along with him, either by the tongue of disposition (lisan al-hal), or by a voice that takes a form for him, or by God Most High creating speech in them. It was also said: they travel with him by swimming. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) to explain the manner of the subjection. «Ma'a» is connected to «sakhkharna» or to «yusabbihna». «Al-tayr» is conjoined to «al-jibal», or is an object in the sense of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu).

It is also read in the nominative (al-raf') as a beginning (ibtida') or as a conjunction with the pronoun, though this is weak. ﴿And We are the ones who do [this]﴾ (fa'ilin), for the like of it; so it is no novelty from Us, even if it is a wonder in your eyes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 80:

﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail﴾ — the making of the coat of mail (dir'). Linguistically, a labus is originally a garment. [A poet] said:

"Put on for every state its garment, whether it be its delight or its hardship."

It is said that they were plates, and he (Dawud) linked and wove them together. ﴿For you﴾ is either connected to "taught" (ʿallama), or it is a description of "labus" (coat of mail). ﴿That it may protect you from your violence﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it, a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion), with the preposition repeated. The pronoun refers either to Dawud, peace be upon him, or to "labus." In the reading of Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs, with the letter ta' (tukum, "it may protect you"), it refers to the craft, or to "labus" under the interpretation of "coat of armor." In the reading of Abu Bakr and Ruways, with the letter nun (nuhsinakum, "We may protect you"), it refers to God, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Will you then be grateful?﴾ This is a command presented in the form of a question, for emphasis and rebuke.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 21, verses 81–82**

﴿And to Solomon﴾ We subjected the wind. The lam (the preposition *li-*, "to") is used here instead of the one in the previous verse, because the extraordinary matter in this case belongs to Solomon and benefits him, whereas in the previous verse the matter manifests in the mountains and the birds together with David, and by its attribution to him. ﴿The wind, violent﴾, strong in its blowing, in that it carries his throne far away in a short time, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Its morning journey is a month and its evening journey is a month﴾. Yet it was gentle in itself and pleasant. It has been said that it was gentle at times and violent at others, according to his will. ﴿Blowing by his command﴾, by his will, is a second circumstantial clause (*hal*), or a substitute (*badal*) for the first, or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun. ﴿To the land which We had blessed﴾, meaning Syria, [it blew him] in the evening, after it had carried him away from it in the morning. ﴿And We had knowledge of all things﴾, so We direct it according to what wisdom requires.

﴿And of the devils﴾ are those who dive for him in the seas and bring out their precious things. The *min* (of, "some of") is either coordinated with *al-rih* (the wind) or is a subject (*mubtada*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is what precedes it, and it is an indefinite qualified noun (*nakirah mawsufah*). ﴿And they performed other work than that﴾, going beyond that to other works, such as building cities and palaces and inventing wondrous crafts, as God the Exalted said: ﴿They made for him whatever he willed: sanctuaries and statues﴾. ﴿And We were watching over them﴾, lest they deviate from his command, or corrupt [things], in accordance with what their innate nature requires.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 83–84:

﴿And Job, when he called out to his Lord: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ (Anwar al-Tanzil: "أنِّي مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ" means "بِأنِّي مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ," that is, "that adversity has touched me"). It is also recited with a kasra (إنِّي), on the basis of an implied verb of saying (إضمار القول) or on the basis of the call (النداء) being taken to carry the sense of saying (تضمين النداء معناه). The word ḍurr (الضَّرُّ) with a fatḥa is common for any harm, whereas with a ḍamma (الضُّرُّ) it is specific to what affects the self, such as illness and emaciation.

"And You are the Most Merciful of the merciful": he described his Lord with the utmost mercy after mentioning Himself with what necessitates it, and he dispensed thereby with stating the request outright, out of gentleness in the asking. He was a Roman, of the descendants of Esau (ʿĪṣ) son of Isaac (Isḥāq). God made him a prophet, and his family and wealth multiplied. Then God tested him by the death of his children, through a house collapsing upon them, and the loss of his wealth, and illness in his body for eighteen years, or thirteen years, or seven years and seven months and seven hours.

It is narrated that his wife, Mākhīr daughter of Mīshā son of Yūsuf, or Raḥmah daughter of Ifrāthīm son of Yūsuf, said to him one day: "If only you would supplicate God." He said: "How long was the period of ease?" She said: "Eighty years." He said: "I am ashamed before God to call upon Him, for the period of my trial has not reached the period of my ease."

﴿So We responded to him and removed the adversity that was upon him.﴾ By curing him of his illness. ﴿And We gave him his family and the like of them with them﴾: that is, he had twice as many children, or his children were restored to life and he had additional offspring from them. ﴿As a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers﴾: a mercy upon Job, and a reminder for others among the worshippers, so that they may be patient as he was patient and thus be rewarded as he was rewarded. Or [it means] by Our mercy toward the worshippers, for We remind them of kindness and do not forget them.

﴿And Dhu al-Nun﴾ and the companion of the fish, Yunus son of Matta, ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ at his people, when he grew weary of the length of his call to them, the severity of their obstinacy, and the persistence of their insistence, leaving them before he was commanded to. It was said that he had promised them punishment, but it did not come upon them at their appointed time because they repented. He did not know the situation, so he thought they had lied to him, and he was angry at that. The form (mughaliba, from the pattern of mutual contest) is for emphasis, or because he angered them by emigrating, since they feared the punishment would overtake them at that point. It is also read as «mughdaban» (مُغْضَبًا).

﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him﴾: that We would not restrict him, or that We would not pass the judgment of punishment upon him from qadar (divine decree). This is supported by its being read in the doubled form (muthaqqal), or [it means] that We would not exercise Our power over him. It was also said that this is a figurative illustration of his state by the state of one who thinks We would have no power over him in opposing his people without waiting for Our command. Or it was a satanic thought that came to his mind, and it was called zann (thought) for emphasis. It is also read with the yā' (يَ), and Ya'qub read it in the passive form (ʿalā al-binā' lil-maf'ūl), and it is read so in the doubled form too.

﴿Then he called out in the darknesses﴾ in the intense, dense darkness, or the darknesses of the belly of the fish, the sea and the night. ﴿That there is no god but You﴾: that there is no god but You.

﴿Glory be to You﴾: exalted above anything rendering You incapable. ﴿Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers﴾ against myself, by hastening to emigrate.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one in distress calls upon God with this supplication except that it is answered for him."

﴿So We answered him and delivered him from the distress﴾: by the fish casting him onto the shore after four hours he had spent in its belly. It was said three days. The distress was the distress of being swallowed; it was also said it was the distress of sin. ﴿And thus do We deliver the believers﴾ from distresses in which they call upon God sincerely. In the Imam (the standard Uthmanic codex) it is «nujjiya» (نُجِّيَ). For this reason the majority (al-jamā'a) concealed the second nūn (ikhfā'), since it is concealed before the letters of the mouth. Ibn ʿĀmir and Abu Bakr read it with a doubled jīm, considering its original form to be nunajjī, so the second nūn was deleted, just as the second tā' was deleted in «tazāharūn». Though this nūn is a radical letter (fā'), deleting it is more fitting than deleting the letter of the present-tense prefix that carries meaning. The difference in the vowels of the two nūns does not harm this, because the motive for deletion is the meeting of two like letters where assimilation is impossible. Deletion is not permitted in «tatajāfā» (﴿تَتَجافى﴾) for fear of confusion. It was said that it is a past-tense passive verb whose subject is a pronoun referring to the verbal noun, and its final letter was made sukūn for lightness. This was rejected: a verb is not attributed to a verbal noun while the agent is mentioned, and the past tense does not take sukūn at its end.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 89–90:

﴿And Zakariyya, when he called to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone, [without an heir], and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ Alone, without a child who would inherit from me. "And You are the best of inheritors." That is, if You do not grant me one who will inherit from me, then I shall not mind being without one.

﴿So We answered him, and We gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him.﴾ That is, We made her fit for childbearing after her barrenness, or [We made her fit] for Zakariyya by improving her character, for she had been ill-tempered (ḥaradah). ﴿Indeed they﴾ meaning those who were so favoured with children, or the prophets mentioned, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿Indeed they used to hasten to good deeds﴾ they hurried toward the gates of goodness. ﴿And they called upon Us in longing and in fear﴾ possessors of longing and fear; or desirous of reward and hopeful of being answered; or [they called upon Us] in obedience and fearful of punishment or of sin. ﴿And they were humble before Us﴾ submissive, or constantly in trepidation. The meaning is that they attained from God what they attained by these qualities.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 93–94:

﴿And they cut their affair into pieces among themselves﴾. He shifted it to the third person (ghayba) by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), in order to censure those who divided the religion and made its affair into scattered fragments, each distributed to others through their evil deeds. ﴿Each﴾ of the factions that formed parties. ﴿To Us they will return﴾, so We will requite them.

﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer﴾ in Allah and His messengers. ﴿Then there will be no denial (kufran)﴾, that is, no neglect. ﴿of his striving﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 95:

﴿And there is a prohibition upon a town﴾ — that is, impossibility (muntani') for its people, which is not conceivable (ghayr mutasawwar) from them. Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-hirmun" with a kasra on the ha' and sukun on the ra', and it has also been read "haramun." ﴿We destroyed it﴾ — meaning We decreed its destruction, or We found it destroyed. ﴿That they will not return﴾ — their return to repentance or to life is meant, and "anna" is not a relative (silah) particle; or it is the non-return of them for requital (li-l-jaza'). It is then a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is (haram), or a fa'il (agent) of it that fills the place of its khabar, or an indication of it. Its estimate is: their repentance, or their life, or their non-resurrection. Or it means: because they do not return and do not turn in repentance. ﴿And a prohibition﴾ — the khabar is omitted, meaning: "and it is forbidden for it, that (i.e., that which is mentioned in the preceding verse)," and the reading with the kasra supports this. It has been said that (haram) means a firm resolve (azm) and a binding obligation upon them ﴿that they will not return﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 21, verses 96–97:

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾ is related to ﴿forbidden﴾ (*ḥarām*), or to an omitted element that the context indicates, or to ﴿they will not return﴾. That is, the prohibition continues, or the destruction continues, or they do not return until the Hour arrives and its signs appear. This is the opening of the barrier of Gog and Magog. *Ḥattā* (until) here is the one after which a statement is reported, and what is reported is the conditional clause. Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read *futtiḥat* with the doubled *tāʾ* (intensive form). ﴿And they﴾ refers to Gog and Magog, or to all of mankind. ﴿From every slope﴾ means a raised ground in the earth. It is also read *jadath* (grave), which is a tomb. ﴿They will swarm﴾ means they will hasten, from *nasalān al-dhiʾb* (the loping of the wolf). It is also read with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*.

﴿And the true promise draws near﴾, which is the Resurrection. ﴿Then, behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will be fixed in horror﴾. The response of the condition is *idhā* (behold, a particle of sudden occurrence), which takes the place of the consequent *fāʾ*, as in His saying: ﴿then, behold, they despair﴾. When the *fāʾ* accompanies it, the two together reinforce the linking of the response to the condition, so it is strengthened. The pronoun refers to the matter (the event), or it is an undetermined pronoun explained by ﴿the eyes﴾. ﴿They will say: "Woe to us!"﴾ is taken to be implied by a verb of saying, and it stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) relating to the relative pronoun. ﴿"We were indeed heedless of this"﴾, meaning we did not know that it was true. ﴿"Rather, we were wrongdoers"﴾, to our own selves, by neglecting reflection and by not heeding the warnings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 98:

﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah﴾ may refer to the idols and to Iblis and his helpers, because by their obedience to them they are in the position of those who worship them. This is based on what is related: when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the verse to the polytheists, Ibn al-Za'bara said to him, "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Did not the Jews worship 'Uzayr, the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels?" Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Rather, they worshipped the devils who commanded them to do so." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾, the verse.

On this interpretation the address is general, and "ma" (what) is taken to mean "man" (those who) or something that includes them. This is supported by what is related: Ibn al-Za'bara said, "This is specific to our gods," or "to everyone who is worshipped besides Allah," and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Rather, it applies to everyone who is worshipped besides Allah."

And His saying ﴿Indeed, those who﴾ serves as an explanation of the figurative usage or the specification, coming after the address. ﴿Fuel of Hell﴾ means that which is cast into it and with which it is fed, from "hasabahu bi-hasabihi" when one pelts him with pebbles; it is also read with a sukun on the ṣād, as an adjective in the sense of a verbal noun. ﴿You are its entrants﴾ is either a new sentence or a substitute for ﴿fuel of Hell﴾; the lam here substitutes for ʿalā (upon) to indicate exclusivity and to show that their coming is for its sake.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 99–100:

﴿If these had been gods, they would not have entered it.﴾ Because one who is subjected to punishment cannot be a god. ﴿And all of them will abide therein forever.﴾ There will be no escape for them from it.

﴿For them therein is groaning﴾ moaning and a intense exhaling of breath. This is an attribution of the action of some to all, by way of dominance (al-taghallub), if what is meant by ﴿what you worship﴾ is the idols. ﴿And they therein will not hear﴾ from the terror and the severity of the punishment. It was also said: they will not hear what would gladden them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 101–103:

﴿Indeed, those for whom the good (al-husna) has already preceded from Us﴾ — i.e., the good quality, which is felicity (al-sa'ada), or success (al-tawfiq) in obedience, or the glad tidings of Paradise. ﴿They will be kept far away from it﴾ — because they will be raised to the highest of the ʿIlliyyun (the lofty heights, the highest station of the righteous).

It is related that ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, delivered a sermon and recited this verse, then said: "I am among them, and Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, Talha, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, Saʿid, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, and Ibn al-Jarrah." Then the prayer was called, and he stood up dragging his garment, saying:

﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ — this is a substitute (badal) for ﴿kept far away﴾, or a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in it, and it is stated for emphasis on their being distanced from it. Al-hasis is a sound that is perceived. ﴿And they will abide forever in what their souls desire﴾ — remaining eternally in the utmost delight. The placing of the adverbial phrase first serves to restrict the meaning and to give it emphasis.

﴿The great terror will not grieve them﴾ — the final blast (al-nafkha al-akhira), in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be struck with terror﴾. Or it refers to the dispatch to the Fire, or the time when it (Hellfire) is closed over them, or when death is slaughtered. ﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ — they will meet them, congratulating them. ﴿This is your Day﴾ — the Day of your reward, which is understood as implied by the word "saying". ﴿That which you were promised﴾ — in the worldly life.

Or it refers to the dispatch to the Fire, or the time when it (Hellfire) is closed over them, or when death is slaughtered. ﴿And the angels will receive them﴾ — they will meet them, congratulating them. ﴿This is your Day﴾ — the Day of your reward, which is understood as implied by the word "saying". ﴿That which you were promised﴾ — in the worldly life.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 21, verse 104:

﴿On the day We roll up the heaven﴾ is governed by an implied *udhkur* ("remember"), or it is an adverb of time (*zarf*) governing ﴿they will not be grieved﴾, or (it governs) *tatalaqqahum* ("they will be met"), or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) implied from the omitted returning pronoun in ﴿you are promised﴾. The meaning of *al-tayy* ("rolling up") is the opposite of spreading out (*al-nashr*), or erasure, from your saying, "Roll up this talk from me." That is because it (the heaven) is (like) a canopy spread out for the children of Adam; when they move on, it is folded up over them. It is also read with the *ya'* and with the *ta'*, and in the passive voice (*li-l-maf'ul*).

﴿As the rolling of the scroll for the writings﴾: a rolling like the rolling of a scroll (*tumar*), for the sake of writing, or for what is written, or in which something is written. This is supported by the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs with the plural (*al-kutub*), meaning the many meanings written in it. It is said that *al-sijill* is an angel who rolls up the books of deeds when they are raised to him, or that it is a scribe who used to write for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also read *al-sajl* like *al-dalw* and *al-sujull* like *al-utull*; these are two dialects of the same word.

﴿As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾: that is, We shall repeat what We created, as a beginning of repetition, like Our originating it, in that both are bringing into existence from non-existence, or gathering together scattered parts. The purpose is to show the validity of resurrection by analogy with origination, because of the inclusion of essential possibility (*al-imkan al-dhati*, the possibility inherent in the thing itself) that makes it fit to be within the scope of power (*al-maqduriyya*). The eternal power comprehends both equally. The *ma* is either a *kafffa* (restrictive particle) or a *masdariyya* (verbal-noun particle), and *awwal* is the first object of *bada'na* ("We began"), or of a verb that is explained by *nu'iduhu* ("We shall repeat it"). Or *ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), and the *kaf* ("as") is attached to an implied word explained by *nu'iduhu*, meaning: We shall repeat the like of that which We began. And *awwal khalq* is an adverb of time (*zarf*) for *bada'na*, or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted relative pronoun.

﴿A promise﴾ is governed by an implied verb, as an emphasis for *nu'idu-hu*, or it is in the accusative governed by it, because it is a promise of repetition.

﴿Upon Us﴾: that is, upon Us is its fulfilment.

﴿Indeed We are ever doing﴾ that, without doubt.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 105–106:

﴿And We had indeed written in the Zabur﴾ — in the Book of Dawud, upon him be peace. ﴿after the Dhikr﴾ — i.e., the Torah. It has also been said that what is meant by ﴿al-Zabur﴾ is the genus of revealed books, and by ﴿al-Dhikr﴾ the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). ﴿that the earth﴾ — i.e., the earth of Paradise, or the Holy Land. ﴿My righteous servants shall inherit it﴾ — meaning all the believers, or those who were oppressed in the eastern and western parts of the earth, or the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Indeed, in this﴾ — i.e., in what has been mentioned of reports, admonitions and promises ﴿is a message﴾ — sufficiency, or a means of reaching the desired goal.

﴿for a people who worship﴾ — whose concern is worship rather than habit.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 107–108:

﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ Because what you were sent with is a cause for their happiness and necessitates the rectification of their livelihood and their afterlife. It is also said that his being a mercy to the disbelievers is that he secured them from being swallowed up by the earth, from being transformed (into animals), and from the punishment of total annihilation.

﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God.﴾ That is: what is revealed to me is only that there is no god for you except one God. This is because the primary purpose of his mission is restricted to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). Thus the first (restriction, "innama"), is for restricting the ruling to the thing (i.e., attributing the ruling to the thing alone), and the second (the "anna" clause) is for the reverse.

﴿Will you then submit?﴾ That is: will you devote worship to God, the Exalted, in accordance with the requirement of the revelation, which is confirmed by proof? You have known that tawhid is among the matters whose affirmation is established through revealed text (sam').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verses 109–111:

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from monotheism, ﴿then say: "I have announced to you"﴾ i.e., I have informed you of what I was commanded, or of my hostility toward you, ﴿on equal terms﴾, being equal in the announcement of it, or being equal, I and you, in knowledge of what I have informed you of, or in enmity, or (the meaning is) an announcement made on equal terms.

It is also said: it means "I have informed you that I am on ﴿equal terms﴾," i.e., justice and uprightness of opinion, by means of clear proof. ﴿And I do not know﴾, and I do not know ﴿whether it is near or far, that which you are promised﴾, of the victory of the Muslims or the Gathering, but it is certainly coming without doubt.

﴿Indeed He knows what is spoken aloud﴾, that which you openly utter of disparagement of Islam, ﴿and He knows what you conceal﴾ of grudges and malice toward the Muslims, and He will recompense you for it.

﴿And I do not know: perhaps it is a trial for you﴾, and I do not know whether the delay of your recompense is a gradual leading on (istidraj) for you and an increase in your being tempted, or a test to see how you will act. ﴿And an enjoyment for a time﴾, and a provision for a set term that His will requires.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 21, verse 112:

﴿He said: "My Lord, judge with truth."﴾ Decide between us and the people of Makkah with the justice that calls for the hastening of the punishment and its severity upon them. Hafs recited "qala" (He said), as a report of the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It has also been read "Rabbu" with a damma, and "Rabbi uhkum" in the form of the comparative (tafdil), and "uhkum" as from al-ahkam (judgement). ﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful (al-Rahman)﴾, abundant in mercy towards His creation. ﴿The One whose help is sought﴾: the One from whom aid is requested.

﴿Against what you describe﴾ of the state of affairs, namely that the power will be theirs and the banner of Islam will flutter for a few days and then settle, and that the promised punishment, were it true, would have descended upon them. So God the Exalted answered the supplication of His Messenger (ﷺ), frustrated their hopes and gave His Messenger (ﷺ) victory over them. It has also been read with the letter ya (yasifuna, "they describe").

And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Iqtarab (Surah 54), God will reckon with him an easy reckoning, and every prophet whose name is mentioned in the Qur'an will shake his hand and greet him with peace." And God knows best.
